120 TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
Mr. Armstrong was appointed on September 19, 1SS7, as a clerk at $1,200
per annum in the office of the Chief Comptroller through the law-clerk examina¬
tion. He was promoted through the various classes to chief of division at
$2,000, and on July 1, 1904, was appointed auditor for the Isthmian Canal Serv¬
ice at $3,600 per annum, the position being excepted from examination. On
May 11, 1905, he was transferred to the position of law clerk at $2,400, Isthmian
Canal Service, the latter position being competitive.
Mr. Armstrong was eligible for transfer under the rules, and the order
merely had the effect of waiving the usual procedure.
March 29, 1907.
One clerk or examiner for duty as private secretary to the Commissioner of
the General Land Office may be appointed without reference to civil-service
rules.
The rules except from examination one private secretary—confidential clerk—
to each head of bureau appointed by the President if authorized by law. No
provision is made by law for a private secretary to the Commissioner of the
General Land Office, and the Executive order granted the Commissioner the
same privilege in this respect as belongs to other officials in a like position.
March 30, 1907.
Mr. James Bronson Reynolds may be appointed a Chinese inspector in the
Immigration Service of the Department of Commerce and Labor without exami¬
nation under the civil-service rules.
The Secretary of Commerce and Labor recommended that Mr. James Bronson
Reynolds, of New York, be appointed in the Immigration Service to make- an
important investigation, and on this recommendation the necessary exception
to the rules was made.
April 3, 1907.
Mr. Jake T. Patrick, a storekeeper-gauger, excepted from examination, in the
eighth Kentucky district, Internal-Revenue Service, may be transferred to a
competitive position in that district.
Mr. Patrick was appointed division deputy collector, eighth internal-revenue
district of Kentucky, September 1, 1S90, and retired from the service June 30,
1S93. In December, 1891, while making an official trip on horseback for the
purpose of organizing a raiding party, he was thrown from his horse, sustaining
injuries as a result of which partial paralysis ensued, and he was subsequently,
and entirely on account of paralysis, unable to perform the duties of division
deputy. He was appointed January 3, 1900, to the excepted position of store￾lceeper-gauger. It appeared that he was noted for bravery in connection with
the raiding and breaking up of illicit distilleries; that his injuries were re¬
ceived while on duty and engaged in an exceedingly dangerous and arduous
task. He is 38 years of age and has had an excellent education, having grad¬
uated from a commercial course at the Ohio Wesleyan University and having
spent two years in a classical course at the Grant University at Athens. His
injuries were of such a nature as not to prevent him from performing the duties
of the classified position of storekeeper.
April 12, 1907.
Mr. John H. McTeer, now a skilled laborer in the Treasury Department, may
be promoted to clerk grade upon passing the clerk examination, which may be
taken before the expiration of the required two years’ service in a subclerical
grade.
The Commission was not advised of the reasons for the promulgation of this
order.

April 25, 1907.
Frederick L. Dunlap, of the State of Michigan, may be appointed to the posi¬
tion of associate chemist and member of the food and drug inspection in the
classified service of the Department of Agriculture without examination and
certification by the Civil Service Commission.
The execution of the food and drugs act required a large additional force of
chemists and inspectors to be added to the Bureau of Chemistry of the Depart¬
ment of Agriculture. It became necessary to create a board to find facts with
regard to the correct labeling of drugs and food products under the law. In
creating this board it was thought wise to bring into the Department a chemist
of first-class basic training and high standing in his profession, who, under the
authority of the Chief of the Bureau of Chemistry, should take part in original
investigation and in the examination and handling of correspondence touching
the topics under consideration. After correspondence with the presidents of
leading universities, Dr. Frederick L. Dunlap, of the University of Michigan,
was selected by the Secretary of Agriculture for the appointment.
April 29, 1907.
Harrison L. Deam, a veteran of the civil war, who has served satisfactorily as
a watchman in the Department of the Interior under temporary appointment,
may be permanently appointed a watchman without reference to the civil￾service rules.
Mr. Deam enlisted as a private on August 12, 1S61, and after passing through
various grades was mustered out of the service January 10, 1866, as a major.
He was temporarily employed for some time in the Interior Department as a
watchman and was found to be well qualified for that position. He is 69 shears
of age, strong, and in good health.
April 30, 1907.
Mr. Nathaniel C. Murray, now a special field agent in the Bureau of Statistics
in the Department of Agriculture, may be appointed assistant statistician in
the classified service in the Department of Agriculture without compliance with
the civil-service rules.
The Secretary of Agriculture recommended the action taken in this case on
the ground that Mr. Murray, who was an unclassified agent in the Bureau of
Statistics, was thoroughly qualified by training and experience to perform the
duties of assistant statistician. It was desired to utilize his services during
the absence of the statistician in connection with the Cuban census.
April 30, 1907.

increase in our work, it is indispensable that the Commission should retain in
its service all of the persons who are capable and efficient in handling the diffi¬
cult and intricate problems which are constantly brought to our attention.
If you think the foregoing facts would justify such action on your part, I

of Mr. McCambridge to the classified service without examination. This would
result in the retention in the service of a highly efficient, necessary, and capable

in a most satisfactory manner.
In view of Mr. Knapp’s statement the above order was issued by the President.
December 17, 1907.
The temporary appointment of Miss Emily G. Stickney as a clerk examiner
in the Bureau of Chemistry, Department of Agriculture, which will expire by
limitation on December 31, 1907, may be extended for such periods as may be
necessary to make an appointment from the editorial clerk examination, which
is to be held on January 8 and 9, 1908.
Miss Stickney was temporarily employed as a clerk examiner at $75 per month
in the Bureau of Chemistry, and the period of six months, for which temporary
appointment may be authorized, would expire on December 31, 1907. There
were no eligibles on the register having the qualifications desired by the Depart¬
ment and possessed by Miss Stickney, but an examination had been announced
to be held on January 8 and 9, 1908. The Chief of the Bureau of Chemistry
urged the continuation of the temporary appointment of Miss Stickney, for the
reason that she had been engaged in the preparation of special reports on food
preservation and their effect on digestion and health, the work being highly
technical, and its completion with the greatest amount of speed compatible with
accuracy was necessary in order to submit the report to Congress during the
month of January.
January 16, 1908.
Mr. Ernest Coldwell, late collector of internal revenue for the fifth district of
Tennessee, who became separated from said office and from the service by the
consolidation of the two internal-revenue districts in Tennessee into one dis¬
trict, may, for the good of the service, be appointed a revenue agent in the Inter¬
nal-Revenue Service without compliance with the civil-service rules.
January 20, 1908.
Mr. James S. Wickham may be employed in the Bureau of the Census upon
experimental work in developing tabulating machinery, as authorized by the
act of February 26, 1907, appropriating for executive, legislative, and judicial
expenses, without examination under the civil-service rules.
This order was issued upon the recommendation of the Commission in view
of the letter from the Director of the Census, stating that the work to which
Mr. Wickham was to be assigned could not be accomplished by the regular force
of the office; that he was a machinist and electrician, and had had seven years’
experience in developing electrical devices; that the need for his services grew
out of the fact that it has been decided to manufacture the tabulating apparatus
in the Bureau’s own shop rather than to have the machines made by outside
parties, which necessitated the employment of a person having not only con¬
structive but inventive ability, both of which w^ere possessed by Mr. Wickham.
February 4, 1908.
Mrs. Isabel E. McKinley may be reinstated in the War Department without
regard to' the length of her separation from that Department.
Mrs. McKinley was appointed to a temporary clerkship in the War Depart¬
ment on December 16, 1898, being one of the temporary clerks rendered neces¬
sary by the war with Spain who were appointed without examination and who
next_page_text:
TWENTY-FOURTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 133
were given the rights of classified employees by an act approved April 28, 1902.
The War Department reported that her service was efficient. Mrs. McKinley
resigned her clerkship on July 9, 1901, and so was not classified by this act.
The Attorney-General has held that a person separated from that temporary
roll is eligible for reinstatement under the civil-service rules. The Commission
recommended that the year limitation fixed by the rules for reinstatement be
waived to allow Mrs. McKinley’s reappointment.
February 7, 1908.
Mr. Douglas B. Thompson, who was separated from the service on the Isth¬
mus of Panama by reason of illness, may be reinstated with the privilege of
transfer to the departmental service if it should appear that any Department
desires to appoint him in spite of his physical disablement.
Mr. Thompson was appointed to a position on the Isthmus of Panama with¬
out examination. While on the Isthmus he took the clerical examination on
December 2, 1906, which he passed. In December, 1907, he was admitted to
the Ancon Hospital, where it became necessary to amputate one of his legs, first
below the knee, and the disease continuing, above the knee. Mr. Thompson’s
name was reached for certification from the clerical examination, which he took,
ancl he was appointed as clerk on March 1, 1907, but was discharged six days
later, presumably because he had not sufficiently recovered from his operation to
perforin the duties of the position. Mr. Thompson was probably eligible for
reinstatement to a position on the Isthmus of Panama, but was not eligible for
transfer to the United States, as he had not served six months after receiving
probational appointment. The above order was therefore necessary in order to
permit his transfer to an office in the United States after his reinstatement on
the Isthmus.
February 7, 1908.
Mr. S. Baillio may be reinstated in the Norfolk Navy-Yard without regard to
the length of his separation therefrom.
Mr. Baillio was' appointed on September 30, 1893, to a position in the Norfolk
Navy-Yard and was classified in his position as clerk on June 10, 1896. He
resigned on March 23, 1906, to remove his wife from the tide-water section in
accordance with the advice of their family physician. Owing to the slow re¬
covery of his wife he did not return to Norfolk within the year of his eli¬

134 TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION.
July 2, 1908.
Mr. Joe M. Johnson may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation therefrom.
Mr. Johnson served continuously in the Government Printing Office as a com¬
positor and proof reader from February 7, 1899, to November 20, 1905, and
inasmuch as he had been separated from the service for more than one year the
commission was without authority to issue a certificate for his reinstatement.
The Public Printer stated that Mr. Johnson is thoroughly familiar with the
work of the office and he believed that his reinstatement would be in the inter¬
ests of the service rather than to try out new material, as the office was not at
that time as well supplied with talent in his line as the Public Printer wished
it to be.
July 16, 1908.
Mr. Herman Gluck, whose services as a deputy collector of internal revenue at
New York were discontinued on March 1, 1907, may be reinstated without regard
to the expiration of his year of eligibility.
Mr. Gluck served as deputy collector in the third internal revenue district of
New York from September 16, 1905, until March 1, 1907, when he was dropped
without prejudice because of his disappearance from home. The Commissioner
of Internal Revenue stated that although Mr. Gluck had been separated from
the service for more than one year the office in which he worked had been
notified before the expiration of the year that application would be made for
reinstatement, but no formal action was taken by that office within the year
limitation. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue also stated that inasmuch
as Mr. Gluck instituted proceedings looking toward his reinstatement within
the year limit he should not suffer a hardship because of circumstances over
which he had no control. The commission not having power to issue a certifi¬
cate of reinstatement after the expiration of the limitation fixed by the rules,
an executive order was necessary for the reinstatement of Mr. Gluck.
July 16, 1908.
George Terwilliger may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation from the service.
Mr. Terwilliger served as compositor in the Government Printing Office from
August 14, 1894, to March 5, 1897, when he resigned. The Public Printer, in a
letter to the President recommending his reinstatement, stated that since his
resignation Mr. Terwilliger has frequently been employed as a temporary com¬
positor, and his service has been highly satisfactory and his record first class.
The Public Printer also stated that he had personal knowledge of Mr. Terwil￾liger’s ability and efficiency, and that inasmuch as he was perfectly familiar
with the work of the Government Printing Office his reinstatement would be
in the interest of the service.
July 16, 1908.
W. S. Lowe, Grosvenor A. Porter, T. E. Brentz, and E. E. Kinnett, of Okla¬
homa, may be appointed without reference to the civil-service rules as experts
in the suppression of the liquor traffic among the Indians.
Mr. William E. Johnson, special officer in charge of the suppression of the
liquor traffic on several Indian reservations, in a letter to the Commissioner of
Indian Affairs, made the following statement in regard to these positions:
The essential qualifications for an officer in this service are honesty, industry,
personal courage, and tact. I can not see how a civil-service examination can
ascertain these qualifications in an applicant. I am very anxious to eliminate
this matter of killing and being killed, which was a factor in my work in the
Indian Territory. The men who were killed down there were all compara-
next_page_text:
TWENTY-FIFTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 135
tively new men with limited experience in such work. The experienced, sea¬
soned men were more able to travel the gait I set for them without these trage¬
dies. For this reason above mentioned, it seems to me to be wise to select as
these four deputies men who are of proved ability and who were conspicuous
in making our efforts a success in the Indian Territory during the past year and
a half.
The Acting Commissioner of Indian Affairs concurred in the recommendation
of Mr. Johnson, and the commission also believed that it was impractical to
fill these positions through examination. The persons appointed as experts
have all had considerable experience specially fitting them for this work. W. S.
Lowe has had a long carreer in the Indian Territory as deputy United States
marshal, railway detective, and deputy. Grosvenor A. Porter has been United
States marshal for several years in the Indian Territory. T. E. Brentz has a
long record as deputy United States marshal in the Indian Territory, and has
been conspicuous in the warfare against boot leggers. E. E. Kinnett has had
several years’ experience as deputy marshal, bailiff, etc., in the western dis¬
trict of Oklahoma.
July 18, 1908.
Mr. William E. Shields may be reinstated in the Government Printing Office
without regard to the length of his separation from the office.
Mr. Shields was appointed as a proof reader in the Government Printing
Office April 5, 1893, and resigned April 9, 1907. The Public Printer, in a letter
to the President, stated that his services in that office were satisfactory in
every detail and his record first class. Since leaving the Government Printing
Office Mr. Shields has had charge of the proof reading on several of the large
newspapers of the country, and at the time of the issuance of the order was
chief proof reader in the office of the Baltimore Sun. The Public Printer also
stated that the proof reading of his office must be improved, and he knew of
no better way to accomplish that end than to secure men who were willing to
resign good positions elsewhere. The President, in a letter to the commission,
stated that from his personal knowledge that branch of the Government Print¬
ing Office needed improvement, and for that reason he issued the above order.
August 27, 1908.
Mr. Harry H. Weddle, of California, may be appointed as inspector in charge
at San Diego, Cal., in the Immigration Service wi

liquor traffic on several Indian reservations, in a letter to the Commissioner of
Indian Affairs, made the following statement in regard to these positions:
The essential qualifications for an officer in this service are honesty, industry,
personal courage, and tact. I can not see how a civil-service examination can
ascertain these qualifications in an applicant. I am very anxious to eliminate
this matter of killing and being killed, which was a factor in my work in the
Indian Territory. The men who were killed down there were all compara-

tively new men with limited experience in such work. The experienced, sea¬
soned men were more able to travel the gait I set for them without these trage¬
dies. For this reason above mentioned, it seems to me to be wise to select as
these four deputies men who are of proved ability and who were conspicuous
in making our efforts a success in the Indian Territory during the past year and
a half.

of Mr. Johnson, and the commission also believed that it was impractical to

TWENTY-SIXTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 128 
work, was in his eighty-first year and not so active as formerly; that this resulted in 
placing a greater amount of labor upon the other special deputy collectors and it had 
been found necessary, in order to keep up with the current work, to assign Mr. Baker 
to duty as an assistant, thus depriving the collector of the services of a private secre￾tary; that Mr. Baker, not being in the classified service, was placed at a disadvantage 
and suffered embarrassment in the discharge of full executive duty as a deputy col￾lector, which conditions could be relieved by his appointment as a special deputy 
collector, this action being in the interests of the organization of the executive and 
prompt performance of current work; that the position under consideration could not 
be adequately filled by competitive examination, the qualifications of good address, 
familiarity with office work, knowledge of the city and its men, experience in customs 
matters, and certain personal characteristics, being absolutely essential; and that 
Mr. Baker, so far as known, had no political supporters, having been selected originally 
because of the record he had made in the department of education in New York 
through the medium of the state and city civil-service merit system. Mr. Baker had 
passed several examinations given by the New York State Civil Service Commission 
and had served nearly eleven years in the state and city governments. In addition 
he had had valuable experience in the offices of large corporations and railroads. 
The Commission joined with the Treasury Department in recommending to the 
President the appointment of Mr. Baker to the position of deputy collector through 
executive order. 
December 9, 1908. 
Mrs. Georgia M. Sargent, widow. of the late Commissioner-General of Immigration, Frank P. Sargent, may be appointed to a position in the classified service without examination under the civil-service rules. 
Mrs. Sargent is the widow of the late Commissioner-General of Immigration, Frank 
P. Sargent. The Secretary of Commerce and Labor in a letter to the President 
urged the issuance of this order for the reason that Mr. Sargent had served the Gov￾ernment faithfully for a number of years, and his failure to provide for the support 
of his family was not attributable to negligence or improvidence on his part. He 
was a very generous man and constantly helped the laboring men over whom he 
presided, and also aided the immigrants at the stations that he visited. 
It was necessary that Mrs. Sargent find employment or become a public charge, 
and inasmuch as her husband had been a prominent government officer the Secretary 
of Commerce and Labor believed it both reasonable and just that some preference 
be accorded her. The Secretary further stated that it was his belief that it would 
be an act of humanity to set aside the rules for the purpose of giving her a position 
and that her case had none of the characteristics which are a menace to the merit 
system and which the rules were designed to eliminate. The President transmitted 
this letter to the Commission with the request that a form for such an order be 
submitted. 
December 10, 1908. 
The executive order of March 21, 1908, permitting the appointment of Mr. Wilhelm Lutz, assistant chief of police of Porto Rico, to a position in the Immigration Bureau of the United States, is hereby amended to permit his appointment to a position in the Customs Service of the United States. 
Mr. Lutz was a sergeant of the Fifth United States Cavalry for thirteen years, was 
honorably discharged, and accepted the position of deputy United States marshal 
for the United States District Court of Porto Rico. Upon the reorganization of the 
Porto Rican police force Mr. Lutz was appointed assistant chief of police, and Gov￾ernor Post stated that he served in that position with absolute fidelity, honesty, and 
capability for five years. Upon the passage of the Porto Rican civil-service law the 
positions of chief and assistant chief of police were not included in the classified 
service, as it was deemed best that the governor should have full discretion to choose

men of exceptional ability for these positions without restriction of law. In other 
words, the importance of Mr. Lutz’s position deprived him of advantages which 
would have accrued to him if he had been holding a classified position and which 
were enjoyed by his own subordinates. ; 
On March 21, 1908, an executive order was issued permitting the appointment of 
Mr. Lutz to a position in the Immigration Bureau, but inasmuch as no opening could 
be found in that bureau the Commission, upon the request of the Treasury Depart￾ment, recommended the issuance of the above order permitting his appointment in 
the Customs Service. 
December 11, 1908. 
Walter R. Gallaher, a clerk at $1,800 per annum in the Isthmian service, may be transferred to a classified clerical position in the United States. 
Mr. Gallaher was appointed an auditing clerk in the Isthmian Canal Service on 
October 24, 1905, without examination, the appointment being based upon his quali￾fications acquired through twelve years of experience in the railroad service. The 
appointment was authorized by the Commission under the executive order of Decem￾ber 12, 1904, permitting appointments without examination on the Isthmus of 
Panama when no suitable eligibles are available. Persons appointed under the pro￾visions of this order are not eligible for transfer to the classified service in the United 
States except through executive order. 
December 18, 1908. 
Mr. Herman W. Kuchmeister, an assistant weigher in the Customs Service at Boston, may be promoted to day inspector without further examination. 
Mr. Kuchmeister served on board U. S. S. Marblehead from November 11, 1897, to 
May 11, 1898, when he was transferred to hospital, Key West, Fla. He was awarded 
a medal of honor for gallant conduct under fire at Cienfuegos, Cuba, having received 
a gunshot wound in the face and neck while cutting a cable, and was honorably 
discharged May 26, 1900. The effect of the above order was to waive the requirement 
of examination before promotion from assistant weigher to day inspector. Under 
the regulation an assistant weigher must serve six months in that position before

TWENTY-SIXTH REPORT OF CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 129 
Mr. Longan was appointed as a clerk at $1,000 per annum for duty as confidential clerk 
in the office of the Postmaster-General on July 10, 1907, under an exception from exam￾ination contained in Schedule A of the civil-service rules. The Postmaster-General 
stated that Mr. Longan had developed exceptional qualifications which made it very 
desirable to retain him as a permanent employee in the classified service, and that he 
was also an efficient stenographer and typewriter, in which capacity he had rendered 
very faithful service. 
March 2, 1909. 
Mr. James Mullenbach may be appointed inspector in charge of information and distribution work, Immigration Service, Chicago, Ill., without examination under the civil-service rules, in view of his peculiar qualifications for the work involved. 
Mr. Mullenbach was very highly recommended to the Department of Commerce 
and Labor as the most thoroughly equipped man that could be found for the position 
in question. For four years preceding his appointment he had been the superin￾tendent of the Municipal Lodging House at Chicago, and prior to that time was for 
two years a resident of Chicago Commons, a social settlement located in one of the con￾gested foreign districts of Chicago. He was thoroughly acquainted with conditions 
in Chicago, had traveled abroad considerably, and through his experience in dealing 
with the immigrant lodger was equipped to render the best possible service in the posi￾tion to which he was appointed. The Secretary of Commerce and Labor urgently 
recommended Mr. Mullenbach’s appointment through executive order. 
Under date of March 30, 1909, Mr. Mullenbach declined the appointment. 
March 24, 1909. 
Mr. F. B. Simons may be reinstated as a clerk in the Bureau of Internal Revenue without reference to the length of time since his separation from the service. This order is made to enable the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to secure a civil servant + with the needed technical knowledge for cases involving denatured alcohol. It is made upon the recommendation of the Civil Service Commission, the Secretary of the Treasury, and the Commissioner of Internal Revenue. 
Mr. F. B. Simons was appointed a clerk in the Bureau of Internal Revenue in 1900 
and resigned in 1906, and was therefore ineligible for reinstatement, as his year of 
eligibility had expired. The Commissioner of Internal Revenue in recommending 
the order stated that although rated as a clerk, Mr. Simons had been assigned as 
assistant in the chemical division on account of his training as a chemist, and that 
his work there was of the highest order, involving the charge and conduct of the 
laboratory in the absence of the chemist in charge, the taxing of oleomargarine and 
renovated butter, and other measures requiring chemical work. Because of his 
experience Mr. Simons would be very valuable in the laboratory of the bureau and 
as an expert witness in connection with the work incident to making analyses of 
oleomargarine and distilled spirits where controversies arise on these subjects and are 
pending in court. 
May 25, 1909. 
Mr. F. B. Simons may be reinstated in the service of the Treasury Department as an analytical chemist in the office of the appraiser of merchandise at Baltimore, Md., without regard to the length of time since his separation from the service. This order 
is made to enable the Secretary of the Treasury to secure a civil servant for a vacant place in the office above named, who is peculiarly well fitted for the performance of its duties by reason of his ten years’ service as a chemist in the Division of Chemistry 
in the Bureau of Internal Revenue. The executive order of March 24, 1909 (No. 1053), authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. irons in the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Treasury Department, is hereby 
revoked. 
April 6, 1909.

the office of the Secretary of the United States Senate from June 30, 1905, to March 31, 1909, may be reinstated in an appropriate position in the classified service. 
Mr Garver was appointed on July 3, 1904, as a forest assistant in the General Land 
Office. He was transferred by act of Congress, with his position, to the Department of 
Agriculture on February 1, 1905, from which department he resigned on June 26, 1905. 
From that date until March 31, 1909, he served as a clerk in the office of the Secretary 
of the United States Senate. Civil-service Rule X, paragraph 3, provides that any 
person may be retransferred to a position in which he was formerly employed or to any 
position to which transfer could be made therefrom if, since his transfer, he has been 
continuously in the executive or judicial civil service of the United States or of its 
insular possessions. As Mr. Garver had been serving in the legislative service the 
provisions of this rule did not permit his retransfer, but there appeared to be no reason 
why he should not logically be entitled to retransfer, and the Commission recom￾mended the issuance of the above order. 
April 7, 1909. 
Mrs. Nannie M. Wayland may be reinstated in the classified service in the Treasury Department without regard to the length of time that she has been separated from the service. 
Mrs. Wayland had formerly served as a clerk in the Treasury Department, but was 
separated by resignation on April 19, 1907. On November 27 of that year the Com￾mission authorized her reinstatement in the Treasury Department, with a view to 
her immediate transfer to the Philippine service. Mrs. Wayland was not transferred 
to the Philippine service under this authority, but did serve for a short period in the 
federal service in the Philippines. Her year of eligibility for reinstatement expired 
on April 19, 1908, and the above executive order was necessary to authorize her rein￾statement after that date. 
April 16, 1909. 
Mr. Archibald S. Pinkett, of Pennsylvania, may be appointed to a clerkship in the Department of State without examination under the civil-service act and rules. This order is made at the request and upon the recommendation of the Secretary of State, who has knowledge of Mr. Pinkett’s fitness from his clerical service under the Secretary while he was a Senator in Congress.
